title: Macrozamia spiralis

{{Short description|Species of cycad}} {{Speciesbox | image = Macrozamia spiralis - Botanischer Garten München-Nymphenburg - DSC08056.JPG | image_caption = ''Macrozamia spiralis'' specimen in the [[Botanischer Garten München-Nymphenburg]], Munich, Germany | status = EN | status_system = IUCN3.1 | status_ref = {{cite iucn |author=Hill, K.D. |date=2010 |title=''Macrozamia spiralis'' |volume=2010 |article-number=e.T41957A10611560 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2010-3.RLTS.T41957A10611560.en |access-date=14 November 2021}} | genus = Macrozamia | species = spiralis | authority = ([[Richard Anthony Salisbury|Salisb.]]) [[Friedrich Anton Wilhelm Miquel|Miq.]] | synonyms = ''Macrozamia corallipes'' [[Hook.f.]]
''Zamia spiralis'' [[Salisb.]] | range_map = Macrozamia spiralis Dist Map24.png | range_map_caption = Occurrence data from [[Australasian Virtual Herbarium|AVH]] }} '''''Macrozamia spiralis''''' is a species of [[cycad]] in the family [[Zamiaceae]]. It is [[Endemism|endemic]] to [[New South Wales]] in eastern Australia, where it is found in [[sclerophyll]] forest on low-nutrient soils. Plants generally lack a trunk and have 2–12 leaves that range up to 100 cm (40 in) in length. ==Taxonomy== [[Richard Anthony Salisbury]] described this species as ''Zamia spiralis'' in 1796,{{APNI | name = ''Zamia spiralis'' Salisb. | id = 265193}} from a collection made somewhere in the vicinity of Port Jackson (Sydney); however, no [[type specimen]] is extant.{{cite journal |author= Johnson, L.A.S. |title= The Families of Cycads and the Zamiaceae of Australia |journal= Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales |volume= 84 |pages= 64–117 [103–05] |url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/34936699 |access-date= 2018-10-26 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160306092729/http://biodiversitylibrary.org/page/34936699 |archive-date= 2016-03-06 |url-status= live }} Dutch botanist [[Friedrich Anton Wilhelm Miquel]] gave it its current name in 1842.{{APNI | name = ''Macrozamia spiralis'' (Salisb.) Miq. | id = 5433}} Meanwhile, [[Joseph Dalton Hooker]] described ''M. corallipes'' from a plate in 1872. For many years, the name ''M. spiralis'' was applied to the large common cycad from the Sydney region, while its smaller relative was known as ''M. corallipes''. In 1959, New South Wales Herbarium botanist [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson|Lawrie Johnson]] examined the species descriptions and determined that Salisbury's original description was in fact of the smaller species, and renamed the familiar burrawang as ''[[Macrozamia communis]]''. ==Description== This cycad is [[wikt:acaulescent|acaulescent]];{{Flora of Australia Online|name=Macrozamia spiralis|id=57464}} the 8–20 cm (3.2–8 in) diameter stem does not generally grow above ground level.{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Macrozamia |species=spiralis |author=L. Murray|accessdate=26 May 2014}} Plants have 2–12 leaves that range from 35 to 100 cm (14–40 in) in length. Each compound frond has 45–120 simple pinnae that are 12–20 cm (4.5–8 in) long at the leaf's greatest width. Each pinna is 0.5–1 cm (0.2–0.4 in) wide. The [[rachis]] of the leaf is often twisted 180 degrees, sometimes up to 360 degrees, though sometimes not at all.{{cite book |author1=Fairley, Alan |author2=Moore, Philip |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District:An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition= 2nd|publisher=Kangaroo Press |page=49|location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-7318-1031-7}} A male plant develops 1 to 4 male (or pollen-bearing) cones, which are fusiform (spindle-shaped), and measure 15–20 cm (6–8 in) high by 5–6 cm (2-2.4 in) wide. The female plant produces a single oval female (seed) cone, which is 12–20 cm (4.5–8 in) high and 6–9 cm (2.4–3.5 in) wide. The orange to red fleshy seeds have been reported to be ripe in April and May.{{cite journal|author1=Benson, Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn |year=1993 |title=Ecology of Sydney Plant Species Part 1: Ferns, fern-allies, cycads, conifers and dicotyledon families Acanthaceae to Asclepiadaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=257–422 [338] |url=http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0004/92902/Ecology_of_Sydney_Plant_Species_Part_1.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110311130303/http://rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0004/92902/Ecology_of_Sydney_Plant_Species_Part_1.pdf |archive-date=2011-03-11 }} Plants do not reproduce until 10 to 20 years of age and are thought to live over 60 years. They regrow from the ground after bushfire. Seedlings of ''Macrozamia spiralis'' have a [[tuber]] and [[wikt:Special:Search/coralloid|coralloid]] roots that rise up above the ground containing [[cyanobacteria]]. These exist in a symbiotic relationship with their cycad [[Host (biology)|host]] by [[nitrogen fixation]]. Field work done on roots of 74 cycads from diverse genera in 2010 showed that the relationship between cycad and cyanobacterium species is not exclusive; the most common genera of cyanobacteria isolated from cycads were those of ''[[Nostoc]]'' (which was isolated from ''M. spiralis'') and ''[[Calothrix]]''.{{cite journal| journal = Molecular Plant-Microbe Interactions |year= 2010 |volume= 23|issue=6 |pages= 811–22 | doi= 10.1094/MPMI-23-6-0811 |title=Host selection of symbiotic cyanobacteria in 31 species of the Australian cycad genus: Macrozamia (Zamiaceae) |author1=Gehringer, Michelle M. |author2=Pengelly, Jasper J. |author3=Cuddy, William S. |author4=Fieker, Claus |author5=Forster, Paul I. |author6=Neilan, Brett A. |pmid=20459320 |doi-access=free }} ==Distribution and habitat== ''Macrozamia spiralis'' is found in central New South Wales, from [[Dunedoo]] and the Goulburn River valley eastwards over the [[Blue Mountains (New South Wales)|Blue Mountains]] and into the [[Sydney Basin]] south to [[Waterfall, New South Wales|Waterfall]], and [[Wallacia, New South Wales|Wallacia]], and north to [[Maroota, New South Wales|Maroota]] and [[Putty, New South Wales|Putty]]. Conservation areas that it is protected in include [[Werakata National Park]], [[Windsor Downs Nature Reserve]], [[Agnes Banks Nature Reserve]], and [[Castlereagh Nature Reserve]], where it is common. Scattered plants grow on clay, sandy or gravelly low-nutrient soils in [[sclerophyll]] forest, under such trees as narrow-leaved apple (''[[Angophora bakeri]]'') and broad-leaved red ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus fibrosa]]''). ''Macrozamia spiralis'' was rated as ''endangered'' in 2003. ==Cultivation== ''Macrozamia spiralis'' is suitable for growing in pots or in the ground, though requires good drainage and benefits from extra water in dry periods. It can be grown under established trees. It can be propagated by seed, though germination takes 12 to 18 months.{{cite book |author1=Elliot, Rodger W. |author2=Jones, David L. |author3=Blake. Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation:Volume 6 – K-M|year=1993 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne, Victoria |isbn=0-85091-589-9|page=379}} == Uses == The plant has been used to produce alcohol, adhesive pastes, and laundry starch.{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Pieroni |first1=Andrea |author-link=Andrea Pieroni (ethnobotanist) |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=36 |isbn=0-415-92746-3}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q5472958}} [[Category:Macrozamia|spiralis]] [[Category:Endemic flora of Australia]] [[Category:Flora of New South Wales]] [[Category:Cycadophyta of Australia]] [[Category:Endangered flora of Australia]] [[Category:Plants described in 1796]] [[Category:Taxonomy articles created by Polbot]] [[Category:Taxa named by Friedrich Anton Wilhelm Miquel]]
